title: Even Birds Get Jet Lag
summary:
New research shows humans are not the only species to get jet lag: some birds appear to experience it too. A study in the journal Science found that Manx shearwaters become slightly disoriented on long Atlantic flights, because their internal clocks fall out of sync with the sun.

Manx shearwaters are a common bird in the British Isles. They look a little like seagulls but are closely related to albatrosses, said Patrick Lewin, a behavioral ecologist at the University of Oxford. Shearwater couples mate for life and lay just one egg, taking turns incubating it: one partner sits nonstop while the other goes to sea.

For up to two weeks, the hunting partners scour the North Atlantic for fish and squid, often hundreds of miles from their nests. Once full, they bomb it back to their colony, Lewin said, often in just a day or so.

That raised an interesting question: do Manx shearwaters feel jet lag, or perhaps more aptly, flap lag? Lewin used 20 years of GPS tracker data from his colleagues on flights out to the Atlantic and back. Shearwaters are believed to navigate by the sun, and using the sun as a compass requires knowing the time of day: east in the morning, slightly south at midday in the northern hemisphere, west in the evening. With the wrong time, they would fly the wrong way.

That is what Lewin and his colleagues saw: rushing home, the birds veered slightly off course. At most, a seven-degree error took a bird about three miles out of its way on a 600-mile journey.

Alice Boyle, a biologist at the Centre for Animals on the Move at Western University in Ontario, Canada, who was not part of the study, called the paper so cool. She said almost every creature must navigate its environment, yet studies showing navigation decisions in action are rare, and wild birds travelling to remote places can teach us so much about how they do it.
why_it_matters: The finding shows that body clocks matter far beyond humans, and studying wild birds in remote places can reveal how animals actually make navigation decisions in the real world.

background_read: Manx shearwaters are seabirds that nest on land but spend long stretches hunting far out over the ocean.
Like many travellers, they seem to use the sun as a compass, and using the sun that way only works if you know the time of day.
Every living thing has an inner clock that keeps its body in step with day and night, and when that clock no longer matches the sun, directions based on the sun can go wrong.
That mismatch is what people call jet lag, and fast, long flights home may leave shearwaters with a version of it too.
